title: Qualitative data analysis methods: six approaches and when to use each
summary: Compare six qualitative data analysis methods by question, data type, and constraints, plus an evidence standard that survives stakeholder review.
body_markdown:
What is the difference between thematic analysis and content analysis? +


Thematic analysis builds codes from the data to explain meaning and the drivers behind decisions, answering "why." Content analysis applies a predefined codebook to produce comparable counts that sit alongside quantitative data, answering "how many."


Can I use more than one qualitative analysis method on the same data set? +


Yes. Sequencing two methods often gives a fuller picture: use thematic analysis to discover themes, then content analysis with a fixed codebook to measure prevalence, as long as you keep the original conversations available for recoding.


What is the biggest mistake teams make when choosing a qualitative analysis method? +


Choosing a method out of habit and fitting the research question to it afterward. Write down the question type, the data type, and the claim you need to defend before coding starts, then shortlist the appropriate methods.


How many participants do I need for grounded theory? +


Grounded theory determines sample size by saturation, and sampling is iterative: you keep collecting until new data no longer changes the model. Theoretical sampling decides who comes next, so plan a fieldwork window wide enough to add participants, and budget time for manual coding and memos.


How do I report prevalence from qualitative data without overstating it? +


Report the denominator, "9/14 participants" rather than "most participants," and count participants rather than excerpts. Pair each count with a verbatim quote and a timestamp, and use quantitative methods on a larger sample for claims about a whole market.
